lesson_6.watch_out: Israeli settlements did not start under Likud in 1977—Labour initiated strategic Jordan Valley outposts after 1967 under the Allon Plan before Likud accelerated ideological West Bank expansion.

passage.bullet: Israeli armour crossed into Jordan in March 1968 → Fatah fighters and Jordanian artillery stood firm at Karameh

lesson_7.watch_out: Karameh was not a conventional military defeat of Israel—IDF troops demolished the camp, yet standing firm against Israeli tanks handed Fatah a decisive propaganda triumph.

passage.bullet: George Habash’s Marxist PFLP challenged Arafat → used international skyjackings to seize global media attention

lesson_7.watch_out: Do not blame Yasser Arafat’s Fatah directly for Dawson’s Field—the hijackings were staged by Dr George Habash’s radical Marxist rival faction, the PFLP.

passage.bullet: Armed checkpoints, illegal taxes, and street defiance in Amman → turned PLO militias into a state-within-a-state

lesson_7.watch_out: Keep the two meanings of Black September distinct—it names both the September 1970 Jordanian civil war and the covert militant cell later created to avenge that expulsion.

passage.bullet: Eight Black September gunmen scaled Munich’s village fence → killed two Israelis and took nine hostages

lesson_7.watch_out: State the casualty figures accurately—two Israelis died initially inside the Olympic Village and nine hostages died at Fürstenfeldbruck airfield, totalling eleven Israeli victims.

passage.bullet: Golda Meir bombed PLO camps in Lebanon and Syria → authorised Mossad’s covert Operation Wrath of God

lesson_7.watch_out: Examine both sides of Munich’s international impact—it revulsed Western public opinion against Palestinian terrorism while making Palestinian statelessness impossible for world powers to ignore.

passage.bullet: Nasser launched sustained Suez shelling in March 1969 → bled Israeli manpower so 1967 lines would not turn permanent

lesson_8.watch_out: Do not confuse the 1969–1970 War of Attrition with the October 1973 war—Nasser waged static cross-canal bombardments, whereas Sadat launched a full canal crossing in 1973.

passage.bullet: Golda Meir and Henry Kissinger dismissed Sadat’s 1971 canal-for-pullback offer → convinced Cairo only war could unlock talks

context.bullet: Lost Suez Canal tolls and huge military budgets drained Egypt → made endless Sinai stalemate unsustainable for Sadat

stems.stem: After Golda Meir and ____________ rejected his February 1971 offer to reopen Suez, Sadat concluded that Israel would never negotiate while ____________.

Behind the scenes, Cairo coordinated a secret offensive alliance with ____________ backed by Soviet anti-tank and anti-aircraft missiles.

lesson_8.watch_out: Sadat did not expel Soviet advisers to abandon war—he removed Moscow’s restraint while keeping Soviet missiles to fight a limited war that would force US diplomacy.

passage.bullet: Attacked at 14:00 on Yom Kippur during Ramadan → caught demobilised Israel off guard after intelligence misread drills

Hundreds of Syrian tanks surged across the Golan Heights → stretched Israeli forces in a two-front existential crisis

context.bullet: Six-Day War triumph and Bar-Lev fortifications bred overconfidence → Israeli commanders underestimated Arab planning and discipline
Dense Egyptian SAM batteries and portable anti-tank missiles → blunted the IDF’s once-dominant jets and tanks
Damascus joined Sadat’s offensive to recapture the Golan Heights lost in June 1967 → forced Israel to split reserves

stems.stem: Launching their assault on ____________, Egypt and Syria achieved surprise because Israeli intelligence misread troop concentrations as ____________.

lesson_8.watch_out: Never describe the 1973 Yom Kippur War as an easy Israeli blitzkrieg like 1967—Egypt and Syria inflicted heavy early losses that shook Israel to its core.

General Ariel Sharon crossed to the west bank of Suez → trapped Egypt’s Third Army and advanced toward Cairo
Soviet threats to intervene triggered a brief US nuclear alert → drove both superpowers to enforce ceasefire

Resupplying Israel then restraining Sharon from crushing Egypt’s Third Army → positioned America as essential mediator

lesson_8.watch_out: Keep the operations straight—Operation Nickel Grass was the US cargo airlift to Israel, whereas Ariel Sharon led the IDF armoured crossing west of the Suez Canal.

passage.bullet: Arab OPEC ministers cut output and embargoed America → quadrupled crude prices, causing Western fuel shortages and recession
UN Resolution 338 halted fighting on 22 October → mandated immediate direct negotiations rooted in Resolution 242
Heavy IDF losses ended Israeli invulnerability while canal gains restored Egyptian pride → unlocked genuine peace talks

context.bullet: Surging early-1970s Western reliance on Gulf oil → made the 1973 OPEC boycott vastly stronger than 1967’s failure
Public trauma over heavy 1973 casualties and intelligence blunders → convinced Israeli leaders Sinai peace beat endless war

lesson_8.watch_out: Judge 1973 both militarily and politically—Israel ended the war ahead on the battlefield, yet Sadat won his strategic goal by breaking diplomatic deadlock and drawing in Washington.

passage.bullet: Henry Kissinger flew repeatedly between Jerusalem, Cairo, and Damascus → pursued practical bilateral pullbacks over grand conferences
Brokered Sinai I, May 1974 Golan pullback, and Sinai II → separated rival armies across UN buffer zones
Israeli pullback enabled Sadat to reopen the Suez Canal in June 1975 → restored tolls and cemented US-Egyptian ties

context.bullet: Demonstrating serious American mediation via Sinai I → persuaded Arab OPEC producers to end the crippling oil embargo

lesson_9.watch_out: Kissinger’s shuttle diplomacy achieved interim military disengagement pullbacks in 1974–1975, not a final peace treaty—full Egyptian-Israeli peace came later under Jimmy Carter.
